title: Can Robots Be Lawyers? Computers, Lawyers, and the Practice of Law
pub: Georgetown Journal of Legal Ethics, vol. 30 (2017)
author: Dana Remus · Frank S. Levy

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The excerpts support adjacent concerns about lawyers’ interpretive responsibilities and clients’ relational needs, but they do not address in-house buyer power, professional capture, reciprocal duties or contextual regulation. They therefore provide insufficient evidence to determine the source’s position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Professional independence: Regulation should follow client vulnerability
st.an: The source identifies conditions for legal effectiveness—voluntary compliance, accessibility and substantive interpretation—but does not address whether regulatory authority should vary by client vulnerability, harm or organizational setting. It therefore informs the cluster’s account of professional functions without taking a discernible position on its principal regulatory proposition.
qs: 1545, 1547-48 (1995) (“In a complex legal environment much law cannot be known and acted upon, cannot function as law, without lawyers to make it accessible to those for whom it is relevant.”); W.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s distinction between accurate output and effective human judgment, while materially extending it with a task-specific account: counseling and fact investigation depend on spontaneous, unstructured communication, emotional intelligence, trust and nonverbal interpretation. It also acknowledges selective automation of components, rather than claiming that whole legal functions are immune to automation.
qs: More broadly, the vast majority of a lawyer’s personal interactions—with clients as well as  with all others—continue to require spontaneity, unstructured communication, and emotional  intelligence.

Some aspects of the task can be automated—for example, software  can usefully pull together vast amounts of online data regarding a client or opponent, and some  lawyers and legal aid clinics automate initial client intake.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central task-reconfiguration account and materially strengthens it with task-level time-use estimates showing that strongly automatable work occupied only a small share of lawyer time. It also reinforces supervised deployment by noting that even automated document review requires senior-lawyer training and review, while treating profession-wide displacement estimates as conditional rather than demonstrated.
qs: Note that only 4.1 percent of lawyers’ time at Tier 1 firms, and 3.6 percent of time at Tier 2-  5 firms was billed to tasks where automation has potentially strong employment effects.

st.t: Online disputes: Faster processing may not improve justice
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether faster online processing improves substantive justice, but materially extends the synthesis by separating theoretical lawyer or judge substitution from actual employment displacement. It also explains that current systems largely address low-value disputes that would not otherwise support legal representation, reinforcing the cluster’s distinction between unmet-need assistance, automated adjudication and lawyer displacement.
qs: Their impact on lawyer employment may be  significant in the future, but we estimate it is minimal at present.

The disputes that these systems  resolve are generally small stakes e-commerce issues, for which it would not be economically  feasible to hire a lawyer and litigate (such that lawyer labor is not being replaced).101 Similarly,  expert systems are generally directed at reaching new markets rather than improving efficiency  in existing tasks).

st.t: Outsourcing fees: Delegation cannot justify double recovery
st.an: The source accepts that outsourcing or automation does not displace the lawyer’s ultimate responsibility, then materially extends the cluster by defining functions that should not be delegated to computers and conditionally linking competent automation to access to justice. It does not address the cluster’s billing or double-recovery rules.
qs: But surely some tasks, such as in court advocacy and settlement or plea negotiations,  cannot and should not be delegated to a computer.
This argument applies to  technologies as well—if they can, in fact, perform aspects of legal practice as well as humans,  shouldn’t we use them to increase access to justice?

st.t: Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s safeguard-oriented approach rather than endorsing wholesale deregulation, while materially developing its technology-regulation argument: professional regulation remains valuable, but existing UPL categories are a poor fit for online legal tools. It offers conceptual analysis, not evidence that provider reform improves access outcomes.
qs: We see a continuing need for, and value in,  professional regulation.
However, for at least four reasons, the UPL rules—the principal way in  which the profession currently addresses new technologies—is an unhelpful approach.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s supervised, task-specific framing and materially extends it by identifying an out-of-distribution failure mode in due diligence and discovery: consequential or atypically worded documents may evade systems trained on ordinary examples. Its licensure argument also reinforces continuing human competence and accountability.
qs: The most relevant documents in a case may therefore use language and tone that many  predicting coding products, trained on a sample of normal documents, will fail to recognize.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core task-level account: automation reaches structured components of legal work while lawyers remain necessary for contextual and consequential functions. It materially strengthens that proposition with large-firm billing data showing limited exposure to strongly automatable tasks and an explicitly qualified estimate of modest near-term reductions in demand for lawyer hours.
qs: Throughout the discussion, we ask how computers are changing – not simply         replacing - the work of lawyers.
Note that only 4.1 percent of lawyers’ time at Tier 1 firms, and 3.6 percent of time at Tier 2-  5 firms was billed to tasks where automation has potentially strong employment effects.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis’s core view that legal AI can expand access and automate bounded, structured work but does not justify unrestricted lawyering or wholesale lawyer replacement. Its account of limits in unstructured communication indirectly supports human judgment and task-specific deployment, though it does not directly examine verification burdens, remedies, inequality or risks shifted to unrepresented users.
qs: Machine learning applications appear poised to displace  lawyers, to make inroads on the profession’s monopoly, and to open new ways of addressing the  access to justice gap.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between task-level automation and profession-wide employment contraction. It argues that supply–demand imbalance and pre-existing labour-market weakness explain more than automation alone, while still treating computerisation as one contributing pressure and allowing future technology adoption to change demand.
qs: Our estimates  indicate that the argument is overstated and that a more important cause is a basic imbalance  between supply and demand.

In 2009 NLJ 250  firms laid off 5,259 attorneys—about 4% of all NLJ 250 attorneys (including 8.7% of NLJ 250  associates).129 If we date the age of legal artificial intelligence to the judge’s 2012 decision in Da  Silva Moore affirming technology assisted review, we can say that to this point, computerized  work has been one of many drags on a generally weak market.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central framing: technology may lower costs and expand access when it performs relevant legal work competently, but protection and accountability remain necessary. It specifically criticizes UPL rules as an ill-fitting technology framework while retaining professional regulation and limits on delegating core legal functions.
qs: However, for at least four reasons, the UPL rules—the principal way in  which the profession currently addresses new technologies—is an unhelpful approach.
This argument applies to  technologies as well—if they can, in fact, perform aspects of legal practice as well as humans,  shouldn’t we use them to increase access to justice?

st.t: Legal automation: Classification success cannot prove reasoning
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between successful automation of narrow, structured tasks and broader legal reasoning or lawyer displacement. It treats document classification and related applications as genuine advances while stressing that they sidestep unstructured interpretation and common-sense inference; widespread displacement remains a prediction under examination.

st.t: Legal computability: Rules never exhaust legal outcomes
st.an: The fragment supports the cluster’s broader claim that legal function cannot be reduced to determinate rules or prediction: it presents procedure, argument, participation and reason-giving as additional values of legal practice. However, because these are attributed scholarly accounts and the excerpt does not establish the author’s overall conclusion, its support for the full claim that rules never exhaust outcomes is limited rather than independently demonstrated.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between bounded predictive capability and sound legal advice. It accepts that prediction tools can outperform humans in some structured settings, but maintains that advising still requires human interpretation, client-specific judgment and reason-giving; it also warns that reducing advice to prediction could impair legal development.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal conclusion that automation has not been shown to cause broad lawyer displacement and that workforce outcomes reflect multiple forces. It specifically argues that supply–demand imbalance is more important than automation and treats computerized work as only one pressure on an already weak market, while not directly assessing the junior training pipeline.
qs: Our estimates  indicate that the argument is overstated and that a more important cause is a basic imbalance  between supply and demand.

In 2009 NLJ 250  firms laid off 5,259 attorneys—about 4% of all NLJ 250 attorneys (including 8.7% of NLJ 250  associates).129 If we date the age of legal artificial intelligence to the judge’s 2012 decision in Da  Silva Moore affirming technology assisted review, we can say that to this point, computerized  work has been one of many drags on a generally weak market.

st.t: Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that predictive coding is a mature, judicially accepted form of selective automation that reduces review labor without eliminating lawyer judgment. It emphasizes lawyer-led training, iterative retraining and case-specific suitability, while its performance and employment claims are not numerically substantiated in the excerpt and it does not materially address disclosure-related transparency costs.
qs: Nevertheless, we note that predictive coding cannot completely displace lawyer labor in  discovery practice for several reasons.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s rejection of wholesale lawyer replacement by finding only modest displacement, and it aligns with multidisciplinary, accountable implementation by advocating regulation that combines legal and technical expertise while protecting clients and legal-system values. It does not directly address substantive verification or task-specific AI evaluation.
qs: First, we showed that  while technology is undoubtedly advancing and changing the nature of legal practice, it is  displacing lawyers at a modest pace.

Instead, we must begin the difficult but important task of                                                                                                    72                       Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2701092 ^Ldesigning more effective regulatory structures that draw upon both legal and technical expertise,  while protecting both clients and the values of our legal system.

st.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that predictive coding can substantially reduce discovery labor while preserving essential lawyer judgment and responsibility. It identifies continuing roles in training, product and protocol selection, defensibility, and classification of uncertain documents, while qualifying efficiency by matter size and product limitations.
qs: Nevertheless, we note that predictive coding cannot completely displace lawyer labor in  discovery practice for several reasons.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition by linking corporate work moving in-house and mounting client cost pressure to greater technology adoption, while identifying billable-hour incentives as a historic barrier to efficiency. It does not develop the cluster’s fuller account of task-level unbundling, differentiated providers, junior training or verification risk.
qs: As long as clients were willing to pay on the basis of billable hours, the need  for technology to increase efficiency was not an imperative.
A second factor promoting accelerated technology purchase is the shift of corporate legal  work from law firms to the corporation’s own legal department.

kp.k: Automation changes tasks rather than simply replacing lawyers
kp.d: Remus and Levy challenge predictions of imminent, widespread lawyer displacement by combining technical analysis, unstructured interviews over 18 months, and billing data. Their analysis concerns technologies available or foreseeable from the 2016 draft's perspective, roughly over the following decade. They acknowledge that this linear approach could underestimate radical innovation, but argue that sweeping predictions require explicit reasoning.
qs: Throughout the discussion, we ask how computers are changing – not simply replacing - the work of lawyers.
The resulting analysis is admittedly linear, risking that we underestimate the likelihood and impact of radical future innovation.

kp.k: Billing evidence is substantial but not profession-wide
kp.d: Consilio’s Sky Analytics supplied blinded invoices for 2012–early 2015, classified through 114 UTBMS task codes aggregated into 13 categories and disaggregated by firm size and seniority. The 2014 invoices alone totaled $2.31B. The authors regard pooled Tier 1 firms with 1,000 or more lawyers as a rough approximation of large-firm time allocation. Limitations include discretionary billing classifications, missing solo practitioners and contract attorneys, excluded non-client work, incomplete firm billing coverage, and changing customers that prevent trend analysis.
qs: Because Sky Analytics’ customer base changed from year to year, the multiple years of data were not suitable for examining trends.
It therefore focuses our analysis on law firm lawyers, primarily in the corporate hemisphere.

kp.k: Illustrative displacement estimate depends on strong assumptions
kp.d: The authors assume hours reductions of 85 percent for strongly affected tasks, 19 percent for moderately affected tasks, and 5 percent for lightly affected tasks. Applied to large-firm time allocation, these yield an estimated 13 percent reduction if technologies were implemented simultaneously, or approximately 2.5 percent annually over five years. These are illustrative calculations, not observed job losses: they assume constant work volume and quality, no prior employment effects, and technological adoption that saves time rather than improves output.
qs: If all the technology above were implemented at one time, it would result in an estimated 13 percent reduction in hours.
Alternatively, the volume of legal services would have to increase by at least 2.5 percent per year to offset automation’s impact in reducing demand for lawyers’ services.

kp.k: Cross-domain analogies calibrate estimated productivity effects
kp.d: The moderate-impact estimate draws on bank exceptions processing, where digital check images and workflow reorganization reduced staffing for constant volume from 650 to 470, a 28 percent reduction. The authors attribute two-thirds to technology to derive 19 percent. The light-impact estimate draws on an electronic medical records study of 42 medical practices over three years, reporting a five percent clinician productivity increase for one standard deviation greater EMR use. These analogies support assumptions rather than directly measuring legal productivity.
qs: A computer-friendly estimate attributes two-thirds of this reduction to the digitized images and one-third to the reorganization.
Findings indicate that one standard deviation in the use of an EMR increases clinician productivity by five percent.

kp.k: Automation exposure does not closely track lawyer seniority
kp.d: The authors distinguish machine complexity from task complexity as reflected in firms’ allocation of work by experience. Junior associates spend more time on document review than partners, but also more on difficult-to-automate fact investigation and communications. Table 3 assigns 56.3 percent of junior associates’ time, 56.6 percent of other associates’ time, and 54.2 percent of partners’ time to lightly affected tasks. The authors therefore reject a simple inference that junior lawyers necessarily face the greatest automation exposure.
qs: The factor that undermines a simple relationship between machine complexity and position within a firm is unstructured human interaction, a skill that has so far resisted automation but that is a part of lawyering tasks at every level.

kp.k: Document review has strong but concentrated employment effects
kp.d: The authors identify discovery document review as the sole strongly affected category. They report studies finding higher recall and precision from many predictive coding technologies than human review, while emphasizing continuing human work in training, protocol selection, defending choices, and classifying uncertain documents. Document review accounted for 4.1 percent of Tier 1 billed time and 3.6 percent in Tiers 2–5; Tier 1's 2012 figure was only 6 percent. The authors suggest prior outsourcing and contract staffing explain much of its already-small firm footprint.
qs: Because of this, we characterize predictive coding technologies as having a strong employment effect on discovery practice.
This would be repeating a pattern seen in other settings where the most routine tasks are initially outsourced and eventually automated.

kp.k: Structured tasks favor automation; unexpected contingencies limit it
kp.d: The technical framework distinguishes deductive instructions from statistical, data-driven instructions. Machine learning can expose tacit regularities, but requires underlying structure and sufficient similarity between training cases and subsequent tasks. From the draft’s contemporary perspective, unscripted interaction and contextual interpretation remain major barriers. The authors consequently expect development to favor relatively narrow tasks whose contingencies can feasibly be covered through training.
qs: Most important, the task being modeled must have underlying, if unrecognized, structure.
Models estimated by machine learning have difficulty processing contingencies that differ significantly from the data on which the models were trained.

kp.k: Due diligence and administration support partial automation
kp.d: The authors rate due diligence and case administration as moderately affected. Contract tools can locate clauses, compare provisions, identify discrepancies, and track workflow, but unexpected legal problems and interpersonal management remain harder to automate. Document management has only light lawyer-employment effects because many applications are longstanding and many displaced tasks belonged to clerical staff or paralegals. Descriptions of particular vendors’ capabilities sometimes reflect advertising, and proposed technical mechanisms are expressly speculative.
qs: Other aspects of due diligence review resist automation because they involve searching for unanticipated information
This is speculation on our part.

kp.k: Document drafting differs from substantive legal writing
kp.d: Automated customization of forms moderately affects drafting inside firms because lawyers already relied extensively on templates. Direct-to-consumer forms could affect solo practitioners and small firms, but the authors cannot establish how much business substitutes for lawyers rather than serves new demand. They classify legal writing as weakly affected at the time, arguing that brief-writing involves indeterminacy, contextual use of precedent, and creative interaction between law and facts that structured sports summaries do not demonstrate.
qs: Whether objective or persuasive, legal writing is very difficult to automate.
Whereas a sports writer covers a settled game structure and a final definitive score, a lawyer often writes amidst indeterminacy.

kp.k: Research tools automate searching, not the entire inquiry
kp.d: The authors trace development from indexed databases to relevance ranking, natural-language passage retrieval, and short-memo generation. They rate legal research as moderately affected because lawyers still formulate and iteratively revise research questions. Their account of Ross’s possible reliance on IBM Debater technology is explicitly speculation. They also emphasize substantial human preparation and training, with experienced lawyers needed to identify errors rather than leaving continuous training solely to inexperienced associates.
qs: It is therefore the search that has been automated, not the entire task of researching precedents.

These problems can be reduced over time with continuous training that refines question-answer links, but such training requires use by senior attorneys and not just young associates who may be too inexperienced to spot the system’s errors.

kp.k: Prediction and expert systems can expand legal markets
kp.d: Prediction analytics and narrowly focused expert systems create moderate effects on legal analysis and strategy, while interpretation and advice remain human responsibilities. The authors report DoNotPay’s parking-ticket application and discuss low-cost expert systems as possible entry services leading to more complex engagements. Online dispute resolution may entirely substitute for lawyers in individual disputes, but its contemporary employment effect is classified as weak because many small e-commerce disputes would never have supported paid representation.
qs: As the parking ticket example suggests, not all users of expert systems would have otherwise used a lawyer.
Similarly, expert systems are generally directed at reaching new markets rather than improving efficiency in existing tasks).

kp.k: Counseling and advocacy retain substantial human components
kp.d: Client advising, other communications, fact investigation, negotiation, and courtroom work are classified as weakly affected in the contemporary analysis. The authors emphasize trust, emotional intelligence, nonverbal information, spontaneous questioning, understanding clients’ broader interests, and counseling compliance. Negotiation tools and online resolution offer bounded exceptions, not evidence that all interpersonal legal work can be replaced.
qs: Third and most importantly, effective advising encompasses more than prediction.
More fundamentally, it is because effective advocacy requires emotional engagement with the decision-maker.

kp.k: Weak legal employment predates widespread predictive coding
kp.d: The authors argue that supply-demand imbalance is more important than automation in explaining contemporary market weakness. They point to cheaper contract review labor by 2004 and 2009 NLJ 250 layoffs of 5,259 attorneys, about 4% of those firms’ attorneys and 8.7% of their associates. These events preceded the 2012 judicial approval of technology-assisted review used as their reference point. They acknowledge that their data may miss effects on solo and contract lawyers.
qs: Our estimates indicate that the argument is overstated and that a more important cause is a basic imbalance between supply and demand.

kp.k: Client pressure and insourcing may accelerate adoption
kp.d: Hourly billing and technology expenditures coming out of partner profits historically weakened firms’ efficiency incentives. The authors expect pressure on rates and hours, together with movement of corporate work to in-house departments, to encourage adoption. They present Christensen-style disruption from lower-end services into more profitable work as a more speculative mechanism, distinguishing it from their firmer expectation that bottom-of-market technologies will exert pressure throughout the market.
qs: As pressure increases to hold down expenses, the purchase of technology becomes more attractive.
A third but more speculative factor promoting accelerated technology adoption may be Clay Christensen’s theory of disruptive innovation.

kp.k: Productivity gains need not translate directly into job losses
kp.d: Beyond the fixed-demand calculation, the authors identify market expansion, new services, quality improvement, and adversarial competition as reasons employment effects remain uncertain. Automation of pro forma work is more likely to reduce hours, while opposing parties may reinvest saved time in additional litigation effort. Simplifying or standardizing legal tasks can also extend automation without technical breakthroughs, but may discard meaningful nuance.
qs: Here, it is possible that the two parties settle into an arms race in which lawyer time freed up by artificial intelligence is used in other activities.
In other cases, however, part of a task will be lost in the simplification.

kp.k: UPL rules poorly address technological differences
kp.d: The authors criticize unauthorized-practice regulation for relying on unstable analogies between software, scriveners, and human advisers; overlooking distinctive machine strengths and errors; fitting lawyer-supervised tools poorly; and sometimes protecting the profession’s monopoly. They also criticize the reasoning in Lola v. Skadden that machine-performable services cannot constitute legal practice. Their objection is not to all oversight, but to regulation that fails to examine how automated performance differs from human work.
qs: Second, analogizing to human approaches fails to appreciate that which is unique and different about legal technologies.
Concluding that a non-lawyer cannot competently and reliably perform a particular task does not establish that a computer cannot help a lawyer do so.

kp.k: Effective oversight requires legal and technical expertise
kp.d: The authors argue that nominal lawyer supervision is insufficient when lawyers cannot meaningfully understand the tools. Predictive coding illustrates the problem: unusual or coded language in highly relevant documents can evade some systems, while alternative training protocols and metadata can mitigate particular risks. Selecting suitable tools and recognizing uncertainty require technical competence, and neither clients nor lawyers can always detect failures. Consumer-protection concerns therefore persist even when automation improves average performance.
qs: At least for now, however, few lawyers are sufficiently knowledgeable to oversee new legal technologies in a meaningful way.
As we return to below, effective regulation may therefore require technical as well as legal expertise.

kp.k: Replacing advice with prediction threatens systemic legal values
kp.d: As a normative and conditional argument, the authors warn that substituting prediction for lawyers could weaken compliance counseling, client-centered advice, reason-giving, and democratic participation in legal development. Opaque models might also encode discriminatory correlations into behavior without users recognizing them; conversely, coordinated design could use prediction to counter bias. The authors acknowledge that future systems may become more capable of suggesting novel combinations of legal arguments.
qs: Reducing advice to prediction would eliminate a core function of lawyering—counseling compliance with the law.
There is also the possibility of the opposite—of technology being used to counter, rather than to entrench, human biases.

kp.k: Access gains require safeguards against unequal legal service
kp.d: The authors welcome technology’s potential to serve unmet civil legal need but reject the assumption that market expansion alone ensures adequate access. Silent errors, limited capacity for novel argument, and unequal access to expensive tools could create or intensify disadvantages. They discuss hybrid human-automated services and law-school projects as constructive responses, rather than treating enterprise cost savings as equivalent to access to justice.
qs: Access to deeply flawed and error-filled legal services cannot qualify as an acceptable, much less desirable, answer to the access to justice gap.
The result could be “a digital divide that institutionalizes a two-tiered system incapable of delivering appropriate justice to low-income persons.”

kp.k: Proportionality should guide regulation and acceptable quality tradeoffs
kp.d: The authors recommend proportionality rather than requiring software always to match a skilled lawyer. Lower-cost, less nuanced assistance may be appropriate for routine compliance or parking tickets, but not necessarily for custody disputes or courtroom representation. They argue that clients alone should not determine all tradeoffs, particularly where inexperienced users face information asymmetries. Regulatory bodies should include predominantly, but not exclusively, lawyers, supported by greater technical competence; a full reform roadmap is left for future work.
qs: For now, we propose proportionality as the guiding principle.
The principle of proportionality recognizes that in certain contexts, lowered quality may be an acceptable and desirable tradeoff in service of increased access; in other contexts, it will not be.
We think there must be a role for regulatory bodies, populated largely though not exclusively by lawyers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Remus and Levy argue that automation changes legal work and modestly reduces demand for lawyers’ time, rather than causing imminent wholesale replacement.
pts.d: Their illustrative calculation estimates a 13 percent reduction in lawyer hours if the technologies discussed were implemented simultaneously, or approximately 2.5 percent annually with adoption spread over five years. They find no strong relationship between automation exposure and seniority within a firm: unstructured human interaction protects parts of junior as well as senior lawyers’ work. Discovery document review is the only task classified as having strong employment effects; case administration, document drafting, due diligence, legal research, and legal analysis and strategy have moderate effects. Document management, fact investigation, legal writing, advising, communications, court appearances, and negotiation have light effects. Predictive coding does not eliminate lawyers’ roles in training, selecting protocols, and reviewing results. Research tools automate searches rather than the entire process of defining and pursuing research. The authors argue that market weakness reflects supply-demand imbalance more than automation alone. Looking forward, they expect advances concentrated in structured tasks, with development influenced by natural language processing and adoption by client pressure and in-house efficiency incentives. Employment effects remain ambiguous because technology can serve new markets, generate new services, improve quality, or release time for additional adversarial work. They also predict risks from substituting prediction for legal counseling, including weakened compliance counseling, reduced opportunities for novel legal arguments, opaque discrimination, and unequal access. They argue for proportionate regulation combining technical and legal expertise rather than either blanket exclusion or deregulation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The employment estimate combines corporate billing data, technical analysis and interviews, and explicitly judgment-based extrapolations from other occupations; longer-term claims rely more heavily on mechanisms and normative argument.
pts.d: Sky Analytics supplied blinded invoices from 2012 through early 2015, categorized using 114 UTBMS task codes aggregated into 13 categories and disaggregated by firm size and lawyer seniority. The 2014 invoices totaled $2.31 billion. The authors supplemented these data with unstructured interviews over 18 months with computer scientists, developers, and practicing lawyers, alongside technical literature, product descriptions, and legal authorities. Their assumed task-level reductions are 85 percent for strong effects, 19 percent for moderate effects, and 5 percent for light effects—not measured legal-sector treatment effects. The 85 percent assumption intentionally avoids understating document-review displacement. The 19 percent estimate draws on a bank exceptions-processing case study, attributing two-thirds of a 28 percent workforce reduction to digitized images rather than reorganization. The 5 percent estimate draws on an electronic-medical-record study of 42 medical practices over three years. Cited document-classification studies support claims of predictive coding’s effectiveness relative to manual review; Da Silva Moore supplies evidence of judicial acceptance in 2012, not a performance benchmark. Billing shares show that discovery review accounts for only 4.1 percent of Tier 1 hours and 3.6 percent of other sampled firms’ hours. The authors use interviews, historical outsourcing, market reports, and pre-2012 layoffs to support their alternative explanation of employment weakness. Some accounts of proprietary technologies are expressly speculative, including proposed explanations of KM Standards and Ross architectures. Claims about systemic consequences draw on legal scholarship, technical limitations, examples, and a hypothetical tax-prediction scenario rather than measured downstream effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The analysis concerns technology available or foreseeable from the November 2016 draft’s vantage point, roughly the following decade, and its quantitative estimate is conditional rather than an observed job-loss finding.
pts.d: The five-year adoption scenario assumes constant legal-work volume and quality, as well as no prior employment effects from the technologies modeled. The authors acknowledge that these assumptions simplify reality and that a linear projection may underestimate radical innovation. They state that legal-service volume would need to rise by at least 2.5 percent annually to offset the modeled reduction in demand for lawyer time. The billing data provide only a rough picture: coding is discretionary, recorded time can be revised, invoices do not capture complete firms, and billed hours need not equal hours worked. Solo practitioners, contract attorneys, and internal non-client-billable work are omitted. Technical limitations are framed as current, not permanent: automation requires sufficiently structured tasks, and machine-learning systems struggle with contingencies unlike their training data. Predictive coding is less economical for small document sets and retains human work. Due diligence remains partly resistant because it requires noticing unexpected problems. Greater experience and training may reduce such limitations; future argument-generation capabilities may also improve. The authors do not quantify direct-to-consumer template displacement separately because it is unclear how much represents substitution versus previously unmet demand. Longer-term market predictions consider a hypothetical unregulated market, then qualify it by the actual influence of professional regulation. Systemic harms from prediction are especially conditional on eliminating lawyers, not inevitable consequences of using technology alongside them.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects vary across corporate law firms, contract and support workers, in-house departments, consumer practices, and people with unmet legal needs.
pts.d: The quantitative analysis primarily covers law-firm lawyers serving corporate clients, with Tier 1 defined as firms exceeding 1,000 lawyers. Junior associates spend more of their billed time on discovery review than partners, but both groups perform substantial work involving hard-to-automate interaction. Contract attorneys’ discovery work is outside the dataset; interviewees suggest growing discovery volume had maintained employment despite partial predictive-coding substitution. Document-management automation often affects paralegals and clerical staff rather than lawyers. Direct-to-consumer forms potentially affect solo practitioners and small firms, while also reaching people who would not otherwise purchase legal help; the authors leave the balance unresolved. Corporate legal departments have stronger efficiency incentives than partnership firms and may accelerate adoption as work moves in-house. Law firms may use expert systems to reach new clients and support subscriptions rather than simply reduce staffing. Low-income people and self-represented litigants may gain affordable assistance but face silent errors, standardized services that miss important nuance, or a two-tier system lacking individualized advocacy. Parties unable to afford sophisticated tools may be disadvantaged against better-resourced opponents. Clients and society may lose compliance counseling, reason-giving, and channels for developing the law if software fully replaces lawyers. Lawyers and regulators consequently need greater technical competence, with regulatory decisions informed by both legal and technical specialists.
